> A world map you can bend, roll up, and lay flat. Not a stiff plaque — every continent tile is a separate piece joined by live hinges printed right into the model, so the whole map comes off the build plate in one piece, flexes like a real paper map, and rolls up to store or travel with.

### 2026-10-18 – What I did this session

**4.63h**

What I did this session

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/cS9KscHhpXWpAjsHTuU1VWQAnI2MBiQy/7e03b22fd38b9d48a4c12b6611e03fa4cd52d2d878b65ab9f383f6f2c657f661.png)
**Goal: get the flexi world map actually modeled in Onshape, from a blank document, on recording.** This session was basically 30% modeling and 70% recovering from my own bad measurements — but that's the session honestly.

### First attempt: the strip ratio disaster

Started recording and went straight into making the first strip without properly planning the ratio. I took the strip width as **4 cm** — sounded fine in my head — but when I ran the math for the full 40 cm trail, that width gave me barely any strips. The whole map was going to be like 10 tiles wide, which is not a world map, that's a Lego. The ratio between strip width and total length was just wrong.

I let it run for a while trying to patch it (scale here, stretch there) before accepting that **patching a bad base measurement is a trap** — every downstream feature inherits the error. So I killed it, rolled back to the original version, and started from scratch. That restart cost me maybe an hour of recording time but it was the right call.

### Second attempt: planned before I sketched

This time I did the boring thing first — wrote down the numbers **before** touching a single sketch tool:

- strip width: **1 cm each**
- slit between strips: **2 mm**
- everything else dimensioned off those two

Immediately everything clicked. The strip count actually made sense for the 40 cm length, and the 2 mm slits are exactly the right gap for the hinge to live in. Lesson I basically already knew from the KiCad week: measure first, model second. Ask me how many times I have to relearn it.

### The copy-paste hell

Assembling the strips was the worst part. My first instinct was **linear pattern** — which in theory is the right tool, but in practice I was fighting it every step: the instance count, the spacing, the direction, one wrong reference and the whole array lands somewhere in space. I wasted a lot of time nudging pattern parameters when what I actually wanted was to just lay each strip down.

So I **got rid of the linear pattern entirely** and went old-school: paste and position, strip by strip. It's more manual, it's slower, but every piece ends up where I actually put it and I can see errors immediately instead of discovering them later in a broken array.

## The map scale problem

When the actual world map got involved: **the file came in at a totally wrong scale** — way too large. The transform tool was another major haul, because the map is the feature that everything else (strips, slits, borders) has to align to. Rescaling it meant re-checking every reference. I ended up pulling in **Gemini to help me work through it**, which got me moving again. Not ashamed — the tool is a tool.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/cS9KscHhpXWpAjsHTuU1VWQAnI2MBiQy/6ea513075584962f3cea1ca755c060fdaca841d9fcbd4e1d1f23b8db4d034c77.png)

### Where it ended up

By end of session: **the map is at correct scale, strips are 1 cm with 2 mm slits, and the layout is fully planned and executable.** Nothing fancy yet — no hinge geometry, no color split — but the skeleton is right, which is the part that would have ruined the print if I'd gotten it wrong.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/cS9KscHhpXWpAjsHTuU1VWQAnI2MBiQy/1f8166b2f13d1b1b729da47a03e487d9ff6dcc44e51711403cb0e213f7684096.png)
